title: What is the difference between Kinesis Data Analytics (managed Flink for complex stream processing) and Amazon Kinesis Analytics (SQL-only queries on streams) — and when do you use each?
shortTitle: What is the difference between Kinesis Data Analytics (managed Flink) and Amazon Kinesis Analytics (SQL-only), and when do you use each

s1_definition.profdef: The two offerings differ in power and programming model. Kinesis Data Analytics for Apache Flink, now Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, runs full Apache Flink applications in Java, Scala, Python, or Flink SQL, giving you the complete Flink feature set, event-time processing, keyed state, timers, complex event processing, and rich connectors, for sophisticated stream processing. The older Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL is a SQL-only service where you write simple streaming SQL directly against Kinesis streams without any Flink code; it is easy to start with but limited in windowing, state, joins, and extensibility, and it is a legacy path. You choose managed Flink for complex, stateful, production-grade processing, and the SQL-only service only for very simple, quick transformations where its constraints are acceptable.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has two tools for analyzing its transaction streams. The SQL-only service is like a basic calculator on the counter: an analyst can type a quick sum or filter and get an answer instantly, with no setup, but it cannot do anything elaborate. Managed Flink is like a full engineering workshop: it can build any machine the bank needs, with memory of each customer, precise timers, and complex pattern detection, and it scales to the whole bank's volume. For a quick tally the calculator is fine, but for the real fraud-detection engine the bank needs the workshop, which is why managed Flink is the strategic choice and the SQL-only service is reserved for trivial jobs.
s1_definition.oneliner: Managed Flink runs full Apache Flink applications with the complete stateful, event-time feature set for complex production processing, while the legacy SQL-only Kinesis Analytics offers quick streaming SQL with limited windowing and state, so pick Flink for anything serious and SQL-only for simple, throwaway transforms.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The two offerings differ in power and programming model. Kinesis Data Analytics for Apache Flink, now Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, runs full Apache Flink applications in Java, Scala, Python, or Flink SQL, giving you the complete Flink feature set, event-time processing, keyed state, timers, complex event processing, and rich connectors, for sophisticated stream processing. The older Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL is a SQL-only service where you write simple streaming SQL directly against Kinesis streams without any Flink code; it is easy to start with but limited in windowing, state, joins, and extensibility, and it is a legacy path. You choose managed Flink for complex, stateful, production-grade processing, and the SQL-only service only for very simple, quick transformations where its constraints are acceptable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has two tools for analyzing its transaction streams. The SQL-only service is like a basic calculator on the counter: an analyst can type a quick sum or filter and get an answer instantly, with no setup, but it cannot do anything elaborate. Managed Flink is like a full engineering workshop: it can build any machine the bank needs, with memory of each customer, precise timers, and complex pattern detection, and it scales to the whole bank's volume. For a quick tally the calculator is fine, but for the real fraud-detection engine the bank needs the workshop, which is why managed Flink is the strategic choice and the SQL-only service is reserved for trivial jobs.

**One line to remember:** Managed Flink runs full Apache Flink applications with the complete stateful, event-time feature set for complex production processing, while the legacy SQL-only Kinesis Analytics offers quick streaming SQL with limited windowing and state, so pick Flink for anything serious and SQL-only for simple, throwaway transforms.

sections.s2_technical:
The managed Flink offering is the full Apache Flink runtime as a managed service. You write real Flink applications, so you get the entire model: event-time semantics with watermarks, keyed state backed by RocksDB for very large state, event-time and processing-time timers, windows of every kind, complex event processing with the CEP library and MATCH_RECOGNIZE, async I/O, a wide connector ecosystem, and exactly-once end-to-end with compatible sources and sinks. It supports the DataStream API for fine-grained control, the Table API, and Flink SQL, and it scales elastically with Kinesis Processing Units and autoscaling. This is the option for production-grade, complex, stateful pipelines, and because it is genuine Flink, the application is portable to open-source Flink.

The SQL-only offering, the original Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL, is a much simpler service. You attach it to a Kinesis stream as an in-application input stream and write ANSI-style streaming SQL with pumps and in-application streams to filter, transform, and aggregate, and route results to a destination. It is genuinely easy for simple cases: an analyst who knows SQL can build a quick tumbling-window aggregate or a filter in minutes without writing or deploying code. But its limitations are significant. Its windowing and state capabilities are far more constrained than Flink's, complex joins and sophisticated event-time handling are difficult or impossible, there is no access to low-level state or timers, the extensibility is minimal, and it does not offer Flink's rich connector set or custom logic. It is also the legacy path, and AWS steers new workloads toward managed Flink.

Choosing between them is about complexity, longevity, and skills. You choose managed Flink when the processing is stateful or event-time sensitive, when you need joins, CEP, custom logic, large state, or exactly-once guarantees, when the pipeline is production-critical and long-lived, or when you want portability and the full engineering toolkit; this covers the vast majority of serious use cases. You choose the SQL-only service only for very simple, low-stakes transformations where its constraints do not bite, where the team wants the absolute minimum setup, and where you accept that it is a legacy product. The senior nuances are these. First, prefer managed Flink for anything you expect to grow or run in production, because outgrowing the SQL-only service means a rewrite, whereas Flink SQL on managed Flink gives you a SQL-like experience without the ceiling. First, note that managed Flink itself supports Flink SQL, so you can still write SQL-style logic while keeping the full engine underneath, which usually makes the SQL-only service redundant. Second, the SQL-only service's simplicity is real but shallow, and its lack of robust state and event-time handling makes it unsuitable for correctness-sensitive financial processing. Third, migration from the SQL-only service to managed Flink is a known path AWS encourages, so starting on Flink avoids future rework. Understanding that managed Flink is the full, strategic engine and the SQL-only service is a limited legacy convenience, and matching each to the right complexity, is exactly what distinguishes an engineer who chooses AWS streaming tools wisely.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India needs a quick, low-stakes stream transformation, filtering transactions above a threshold into an alert stream, which an analyst could build in minutes. This is the kind of simple job the SQL-only service can handle, where its limits do not matter.

Problem 2 — The bank also needs a stateful, event-time fraud engine with per-account windows, sequence pattern detection, and exactly-once guarantees, which the SQL-only service cannot do. This requires managed Flink's full feature set.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that models the capability gap and a decision rule, without touching AWS. We define a `ProcessingRequirement` describing a job's needs, namely whether it needs keyed state, event-time windows, joins or CEP, and exactly-once, a `SqlOnlyService` and a `ManagedFlinkService` each declaring which capabilities they support, and a `ServiceSelector` that picks the right service for a requirement and explains why. A `KdaComparisonDemo` main class evaluates both a simple filter job and a complex fraud job and prints which service each should use and the reason, making the when-to-use-which boundary concrete.

```bash

# Run the demo
java -cp target/kda-flink-vs-sql-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.kda.compare.KdaComparisonDemo

# Real: create a managed Flink app for complex jobs
aws kinesisanalyticsv2 create-application --runtime-environment FLINK-1_18 ...
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is two job requirements: a simple high-value filter and a complex fraud engine, each evaluated by the selector against the two services' capabilities.

Step 1. The high-value filter requirement is examined. It needs no keyed state, no event-time windows, no joins or complex event processing, and no exactly-once guarantee; it is just a filter. The selector's complexity check returns false.

Step 2. Because the filter is simple, the selector checks whether the SQL-only service can satisfy it. It can, since a filter is within its reach. The selector picks the SQL-only service and logs that the job is simple. This is the one scenario where the legacy SQL-only service is a reasonable choice: minimal setup for a trivial transform.

Step 3. The fraud engine requirement is examined. It needs keyed per-account state, event-time windows, sequence pattern detection, and exactly-once guarantees. The selector's complexity check returns true because several of these are set.

Step 4. Because the fraud engine is complex, the selector does not even consider the SQL-only service, which lacks rich state, proper event-time windowing, complex event processing, and robust exactly-once. It picks managed Flink, which supports all four capabilities, and logs the reason.

Step 5. The selector reports both decisions. The simple filter goes to the SQL-only service and the fraud engine goes to managed Flink. The journey makes the boundary concrete: the SQL-only service is acceptable only for simple, low-stakes transforms, while anything stateful, event-time sensitive, or correctness-critical must use managed Flink.

```
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    'high-value-filter' is simple -> Kinesis Analytics SQL-only (legacy)
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    DECISION high-value-filter => Kinesis Analytics SQL-only (legacy)
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    'fraud-engine' is complex (state/window/join/eos) -> Managed Service for Apache Flink
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    DECISION fraud-engine => Managed Service for Apache Flink
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The two AWS offerings differ in power and programming model. Kinesis Data Analytics for Apache Flink, now Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, runs full Apache Flink applications in Java, Scala, Python, or Flink SQL, giving me the complete Flink feature set: event-time processing with watermarks, keyed state backed by RocksDB for large state, timers, every kind of window, complex event processing with CEP and MATCH_RECOGNIZE, async I/O, a rich connector ecosystem, and exactly-once end-to-end with compatible sources and sinks. The older Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL is a SQL-only service where I write simple streaming SQL directly against Kinesis streams with no Flink code; it is easy to start with but limited in windowing, state, joins, and extensibility, and it is a legacy path that AWS steers new workloads away from.

Choosing between them is about complexity, longevity, and skills. I choose managed Flink when the processing is stateful or event-time sensitive, when I need joins, CEP, custom logic, large state, or exactly-once guarantees, or when the pipeline is production-critical and long-lived, which covers the vast majority of serious use cases, and I also get portability because the code is genuine Flink. I choose the SQL-only service only for very simple, low-stakes transforms where its constraints do not bite and the team wants the absolute minimum setup. The senior points I stress are that managed Flink itself supports Flink SQL, so I can still write SQL-style logic while keeping the full engine underneath, which usually makes the SQL-only service redundant; that the SQL-only service's simplicity is real but shallow and its weak state and event-time handling make it unsuitable for correctness-sensitive financial processing; and that outgrowing the SQL-only service means a rewrite, so starting on managed Flink avoids future rework along the migration path AWS already encourages.

At the National Bank of India I applied exactly this reasoning. For a quick, low-stakes job that simply filtered high-value transactions into an alert stream, the SQL-only service was acceptable and an analyst could stand it up in minutes without deploying code. But for our real fraud engine, which needed per-account keyed state, event-time windows, sequence pattern detection, and exactly-once guarantees, the SQL-only service simply could not do it, so I built it as a full Flink application on the managed Flink service, keeping the option to express parts of it in Flink SQL while retaining the complete engine. I generally defaulted new, production-bound work to managed Flink even when it started simple, precisely because growth would otherwise force a rewrite. Being able to explain that managed Flink is the full strategic engine and the SQL-only service is a limited legacy convenience, and to match each to the right level of complexity with a concrete example of each, is exactly what shows I choose AWS streaming tools with real judgment rather than by default.
